title: Why Student Behaviors Are Soaring (And What We Missed Along the Way)
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Kevin Stinehart, a veteran public school teacher, argues that the surge in meltdowns and immature behavior in upper-elementary classrooms is not moral decline or poor discipline but developmental delay. He opens with a third grader sobbing over a glue stick and reframes such moments as evidence that children are internally younger than their age. He contrasts the unsupervised, risky, peer-driven play of earlier generations with today's adult-directed childhood. From this he names the Play Deprivation Delay Theory: milestones that free play once completed by first grade are simply postponed until third grade or later. He argues schools have fixated on learning loss while missing this developmental gap. His remedy is practice rather than punishment, meaning restored recess, free play, boredom and small risks, and he reports that kids catch up quickly when given them.
points: Behavior problems in older students are reframed as unfinished social and emotional development rather than defiance, parenting failure or moral decline.
The Play Deprivation Delay Theory holds that developmental benchmarks free play would complete are postponed, reappearing in third grade or later.
Schools measured learning loss in test scores while overlooking a generation's delayed emotional development.
The author's fix is restoring free play, recess, boredom and small risks, because development must be practiced, not punished into place.
He reports from his own classroom that children given these conditions grow by years in regulation, courage and friendship.
quotes: Most of these kids aren’t acting younger because they “just want attention” or because they “don’t know how to behave.” They’re acting younger because in many ways they ARE younger internally. Socially, emotionally, and cognitively, they are extremely underdeveloped.

You can’t wire a nervous system for conflict resolution if every conflict is adjudicated by an adult. You can’t build frustration tolerance if every correction triggers panic. You can’t develop autonomy if every decision is made on your behalf.
We’ve spent years debating “learning loss.” We’ve obsessed over academic regression. We’ve compared test scores and reading levels and math skills like they’re the only indicators of progress.

The emotional work (the messy, vital, hard, beautiful work of early childhood) simply didn’t get enough time and space. And when children don’t get enough authentic, peer-driven, unstructured play in the early years, they don’t develop the social and emotional fluencies that used to be completed by kindergarten or first grade.
Play teaches children to regulate emotions because frustration is built in. Play teaches problem-solving because kids disagree constantly. Play teaches agency because no one tells them what to do.
We can’t fix development with punishment. We have to fix it with practice. And play is the practice.
Kids aren’t misbehaving. They’re trying to grow in soil that doesn’t support growth. But the soil can change.
